strengths: The geometry-grounded BPE formulation is an interesting contribution: observed motif medoids, hierarchical merging, and boundary-angle refinement offer interpretable, variable-length structural tokens.
The glue-refinement ablation provides concrete evidence for a useful component: removing refinement increases average RMSD from 1.66 to 4.39 Å (Appendix A).

Evaluation spans reconstruction, held-out structures, generation, and 24 downstream splits. Several downstream gains are substantial, and the reduced-data experiment suggests that vocabulary learning can be economical when combined with pretrained features.
weaknesses: Downstream comparisons do not isolate the tokenizer contribution. GEOBPE adds an up–down Tree-LSTM to ESM3 features, whereas competing tokenizers supply their encoder representations. Parameter-matched controls using the same features with random, balanced, sequence-based, or secondary-structure trees are missing. Consequently, the gains cannot be confidently attributed to the learned geometric vocabulary. The 1%-data result also retains the extensively pretrained feature extractor.

The generation claim materially contradicts the results. Section 5 describes '99% unique and designable backbones,' but Table 7 reports only 3–4% designability and mean scTM of 0.267–0.277; 98–99% refers to uniqueness. Only 100 samples are evaluated per setting, and comparisons exclude stronger pretrained tokenizers. These results support a limited proof of concept, not convincing generative quality.

The domain-alignment evaluation does not establish functional token discovery. Appendix F selects the best arbitrary consecutive union of predicted segments separately for each ground-truth domain. Fine segmentations can therefore achieve near-perfect scores without meaningful individual motifs; single-residue segmentation would score perfectly. Moreover, Table 2 describes comparison percentiles against random partitions, while Appendix F says parentheses contain random-average scores. This ambiguity and the permissive matching undermine the interpretation of the reported 0.996 F1.

Compression advantages require clearer accounting. Although BPR includes tokenizer description length, the experiments do not provide a reproducible breakdown of model storage, motif coordinates, glue tokens, numerical precision, and amortization. Figure 3's very large BPR values for neural tokenizers make that distinction consequential. Separate encoded-stream and model-storage costs, evaluated at matched distortion and multiple corpus sizes, are needed to substantiate the headline compression claims.

The geometric specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3.1 defines G_i = F_{i+1} F_i^{-1}, while Algorithm 10 uses F_{i+1} = F_i G_i; these require different transform conventions. Algorithm 10 also changes the glue variables from omega to psi and optimizes all residue links, whereas the stated representation preserves fixed motif interiors and optimizes inter-motif boundaries. It is therefore unclear whether the implemented refinement preserves exact codebook-decodable motifs.

Important reproducibility and evaluation controls are absent or unclear: downstream training details and feature modalities, repeated-run uncertainty, practical tokenizer training/inference timings, and a complete fixed-vocabulary inference procedure. Extensive pseudocode helps, but its inconsistencies and the missing code URL prevent resolving these issues.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. GEOBPE does not consistently outperform alternatives across downstream splits, and continuous baselines remain stronger on average flexibility prediction. Low test/train distortion ratios alone do not establish superior OOD reconstruction when absolute errors differ. The expert case studies infer specific biochemical functions from selected backbone fragments without controlled validation, despite the tokenizer excluding sequence and side chains.

strengths: The geometric BPE formulation is interesting: empirical motif prototypes, variable-length hierarchical merging, and boundary-angle refinement provide a potentially useful alternative to learned vector codebooks.
The glue-refinement ablation provides concrete evidence for an important component: removing refinement increases RMSD from 1.66 to 4.39 Å (Appendix A).

The evaluation covers reconstruction, held-out structures, downstream prediction, and generation. Several downstream improvements are substantial, and the 1%-data experiment suggests that useful hierarchies can be learned from relatively few structures.
The extensive pseudocode and hyperparameter appendix make a meaningful effort toward reproducibility.
weaknesses: The generation claim is materially contradicted by the results. Section 5 describes '99% unique and designable backbones,' but Table 7 reports only 3–4% designability, with mean scTM of 0.267–0.277; 98–99% refers to uniqueness alone. With only 100 samples and baselines at 1% designability, this provides weak evidence for useful backbone generation. Uniqueness among largely non-designable outputs does not establish generative quality.

Downstream comparisons do not isolate the tokenizer's contribution. GEOBPE uses ESM3 features plus a parameterized upward/downward Tree-LSTM, whereas competing tokenizers supply their own representations. Missing controls include the same ESM3 features with capacity-matched sequence aggregation and random, balanced, or secondary-structure-based trees. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed specifically to the learned geometric vocabulary. Results also lack uncertainty estimates; the functional-task average is only 79.93 versus 79.82 for MIF, and GEOBPE trails continuous baselines on average flexibility prediction.

The domain-alignment evaluation does not substantiate near-perfect functional token discovery. Appendix F selects, using each ground-truth domain, the best consecutive union of predicted segments. Arbitrarily fine segmentation can therefore achieve perfect alignment without discovering meaningful domains. Direct boundary evaluation and controls matched for segment-length distribution are needed. Reporting is also inconsistent: Table 2 describes parenthesized numbers as percentages of random segmentations beaten, while Appendix F defines them as random-baseline average scores.

The central compression comparison is insufficiently auditable. BPR includes the amortized description length of the entire tokenizer, but the manuscript does not specify a reproducible storage accounting for neural weights, motif coordinates, numerical precision, and glue tokens, or separate model overhead from encoded-stream cost. Algorithms 14–15 require three glue tokens per motif boundary, making this distinction essential. Figure 3 also compares different distortion levels: the reported 18–25% LDDT reductions are substantial and do not establish the abstract's claim of more than 10× compression at similar distortion.

The geometric specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3.1 defines G_i = F_{i+1} F_i^{-1}, whereas subsequent forward kinematics uses F_{i+1} = F_i G_i; these conventions are incompatible in general, and the former transform is not determined solely by invariant internal coordinates. Algorithm 10 substitutes psi for omega in the glue variables and optimizes all residue links, while the method requires fixed motif interiors and optimization only at motif boundaries. The implementation must clarify these choices and demonstrate reconstruction from the serialized tokens alone.

The broad generalization and data-efficiency claims exceed the evidence. A small test/train distortion ratio can reflect a higher training-error floor rather than superior absolute reconstruction. The abstract reports ratios of 1.0–1.1, while the results give 1.16–1.28. Furthermore, the 1%-data result concerns downstream performance using pretrained ESM3 features; it does not establish comparable data efficiency for reconstruction or for the full representation-learning pipeline.

Interpretability evidence is largely anecdotal. Backbone-only motifs are assigned specific biochemical roles involving side chains without systematic enrichment tests or a documented expert-assessment protocol. More generally, downstream training details, measured tokenizer runtime and memory, and variability across runs are insufficiently reported. These gaps, together with the unsupported headline claims and missing controls, prevent the promising idea from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The central idea is promising: extending BPE to variable-length geometric motifs through medoid clustering and hierarchical merging offers an interpretable alternative to learned vector codebooks.

Combining local quantization with global geometric refinement addresses a real difficulty in reconstructing structures from discrete fragments. The refinement ablation provides concrete evidence: removing it increases average RMSD from 1.66 to 4.39.

The evaluation covers reconstruction, held-out structures, downstream prediction, vocabulary utilization, and generation. Several downstream gains are substantial, particularly for binding-site prediction and remote-homology classification.

The appendices provide extensive pseudocode, hyperparameter descriptions, and useful data-efficiency experiments. Maintaining downstream performance with 1% of the tokenizer-training data is an encouraging result.
weaknesses: The downstream comparisons do not isolate the contribution of the learned geometric hierarchy. GEOBPE adds a trainable bidirectional Tree-LSTM to ESM3 features, whereas competing tokenizers are evaluated through their encoder representations. Parameter-matched aggregation baselines, random or balanced trees, and conventional structural segmentations are missing. Consequently, the improvements could partly reflect added contextual modeling capacity rather than the proposed tokenizer. Results also do not support uniformly superior performance: average flexibility correlation is 45.26 versus ProteinMPNN's 54.41, and average functional AUROC is only 79.93 versus MIF's 79.82, without uncertainty estimates.

The generation narrative materially contradicts the reported results. Section 5 describes '99% unique and designable backbones,' but Table 7 reports 98–99% uniqueness and only 3–4% designability, with mean scTM of 0.267–0.277. These results demonstrate a limited proof of concept, not reliable generation of designable structures. Evaluating only 100 samples, without repeated runs or stronger tokenizer baselines, further limits the conclusions.

The domain-alignment evaluation is insufficient to establish functional interpretability. Appendix F selects the best consecutive union of predicted segments separately for each ground-truth domain. Fine segmentations can therefore obtain near-perfect overlap without recovering meaningful domain boundaries; single-residue segmentation would score perfectly. Moreover, Table 2 describes parenthesized values as random-baseline percentiles, whereas Appendix F defines them as random-baseline averages. This ambiguity must be resolved, and direct boundary or hierarchy-aware comparisons are needed before interpreting the scores as biological discovery.

Compression gains are not adequately documented. BPR includes the tokenizer's description length, making comparisons sensitive to the corpus size over which model storage is amortized. The paper does not provide an auditable breakdown of model/codebook storage, motif indices, and the three glue-angle tokens required at every motif boundary. Separate payload and model-storage results, with explicit precision and amortization assumptions, are necessary. The abstract's greater-than-10× reduction at similar distortion also overstates the ProToken comparison: the main text reports 0.271–0.358× BPR alongside an 18–22% LDDT decrease.

The mathematical specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3.1 defines link transforms as G_i = F_{i+1} F_i^{-1}, but subsequent forward kinematics uses F_{i+1} = F_i G_i, which requires a different convention. Algorithm 10 changes the glue triplet from theta/omega/phi to theta/psi/phi and optimizes all residue links, rather than explicitly restricting optimization to inter-motif boundaries. If internal motif angles are changed, fixed medoid tokens need not reproduce the optimized structures. These issues require clarification and verification that reported reconstruction scores come from decoding the final discrete representation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive pseudocode. The submitted manuscript's code-availability statement contains no link, and downstream training details and key inverse-kinematics settings are insufficiently specified. Runtime and memory measurements for vocabulary learning and inference are also missing, making practical scalability difficult to assess.

Overall, the method has potential, but unresolved evaluation confounds, inconsistent algorithm definitions, and claims that exceed the reported evidence prevent the submission from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The combination of hierarchical motif merging, observed-fragment medoids, and inverse-kinematics correction is an interesting approach to interpretable, variable-resolution protein structure tokenization.

The evaluation covers reconstruction, held-out generalization, downstream prediction, generation, and biological interpretation. Reported reconstruction results on CAMEO/CASP14 and tokenization of 550K structures provide useful evidence of applicability.

The appendix provides extensive pseudocode, hyperparameter studies, runtime measurements, and data-efficiency experiments. Downstream improvements on several binding-site and homology tasks are substantial.
weaknesses: The downstream experiments do not isolate the tokenizer's contribution. GEOBPE-TRANSFER adds a trainable upward/downward Tree-LSTM to ESM3 features, whereas the tokenizer baselines use their encoder representations. Without capacity-matched sequence models and random, balanced, or secondary-structure-derived trees, improvements cannot be attributed specifically to the learned geometric vocabulary. Architecture independence is also demonstrated with only one pretrained feature extractor.

The compression claim needs more transparent accounting. BPR includes the amortized description length of the entire tokenizer, making comparisons sensitive to corpus size and neural-model storage. The paper does not provide a reproducible breakdown separating model/codebook storage, motif indices, and boundary-angle tokens. Reporting payload-only rates and corpus-size dependence is essential. Furthermore, the reported 18–25% LDDT reduction is substantial and does not convincingly support the abstract's claim of similar distortion.

The near-perfect functional-domain alignment is overstated. Appendix G selects the consecutive block of predicted segments that maximizes overlap with each known domain. Fine segmentations can therefore achieve excellent scores without discovering domain boundaries or functional units. Boundary-specific and granularity-matched controls are needed. The reporting is also inconsistent: Table 2 describes parentheses as random-baseline percentiles, whereas Appendix G defines them as average random scores.

The generation narrative contradicts the results: Section 5 claims 99% unique and designable backbones, but Table 11 reports only 3–4% designability, with 98–99% uniqueness. With just 100 samples, the improvement over 1% baseline designability is weak evidence without uncertainty estimates. The scaling experiment also changes the length protocol from approximately 214 residues to 50–128 residues, confounding the claimed benefit of increased data and model size.

The geometric formulation contains consequential inconsistencies. With frames defined by world-coordinate axes and origins, the stated relative transform F_{i+1} F_i^{-1} depends on the global coordinate frame; the later forward-kinematics equations instead use right-composed local transforms. Glue variables also change from omega to psi in Algorithm 12. These inconsistencies leave the actual implemented geometry insufficiently specified.

Several broad claims exceed the evidence. GEOBPE does not consistently outperform the strongest baselines across tasks: its average flexibility correlation is 45.26 versus ProteinMPNN's 54.41, and it loses on multiple individual splits. Near-unit test/train distortion ratios alone do not establish superior generalization when training distortion differs. The downstream data-efficiency claim also depends on ESM3 features whose pretraining cost is excluded.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix: downstream optimization and capacity-matching details are insufficient, the manuscript's code-availability statement has no link, and principal comparisons lack repeated-run variability or confidence intervals. These gaps, together with the evaluation confounds, prevent the promising method from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The geometry-grounded BPE formulation is an interesting contribution: observed motif medoids provide explicit geometric meaning, while hierarchical merging enables variable-length structural representations.
The glue-refinement ablation provides concrete evidence for an important component: removing refinement increases RMSD from 1.66 to 4.39 Å (Appendix A).

The evaluation is broad, covering reconstruction, held-out structures, downstream prediction, generation, and interpretability. Small-data experiments and tokenization of 550K structures provide encouraging evidence of practical applicability.
weaknesses: The compression headline is insufficiently supported. BPR includes amortized encoder/decoder storage, so comparisons depend strongly on corpus size and model serialization; the paper does not adequately specify or separate these costs from encoded-data costs. Table 16 reports approximately 36–48 bits/residue for GeoBPE, whereas a 4096-code, one-token-per-residue representation requires 12 bits/residue before model overhead. Thus, the reported advantage over ESM3 does not establish better token-stream compression. Moreover, the reported 18–25% LDDT reductions do not convincingly support the abstract's claim of similar distortion.

The downstream evaluation does not isolate the contribution of the learned hierarchy. GeoBPE-TRANSFER adds a trainable up–down TreeLSTM to ESM3 features, but lacks matched-capacity controls using random trees, balanced trees, fixed segments, or conventional contextual aggregation. Improvements could arise from additional supervised computation rather than the geometric vocabulary. Results also lack uncertainty estimates, and the claim of consistent superiority overlooks substantial losses on repeat prediction and several flexibility splits.

The interpretability metric cannot establish that individual tokens recover functional domains. Appendix G selects the best consecutive union of segments separately for each annotated domain. Arbitrarily fine segmentation can therefore achieve perfect agreement without discovering meaningful motifs. Although random partitions are evaluated, their reporting is contradictory: Table 2 describes parenthesized values as random-baseline percentiles, whereas Appendix G defines them as random-average scores. Strong functional conclusions require direct boundary or motif-level evidence.

There are substantial reporting inconsistencies. Section 5 states that generation produces '99% unique and designable backbones,' but Table 11 reports only 3–4% designability for the main GeoBPE models. The secondary-structure discussion reports 98.28% block recall, while Table 9 gives 31.68 with 98.28 in parentheses. Table 8 also exactly repeats the first five dataset columns in the last five across its metrics. These issues undermine confidence in the quantitative interpretation and require an audit.

The geometric specification is internally inconsistent. Section 3.1 defines G_i = F_{i+1} F_i^{-1}, but subsequent forward kinematics uses F_{i+1} = F_i G_i, which requires the opposite relative-frame convention. The stated G_i also changes by conjugation under a global rigid transformation, contrary to its characterization as depending only on internal geometry. Algorithm 12 changes the glue-angle definition and optimizes every residue link, leaving unclear whether internal motif geometry remains fixed after merging. These are material ambiguities for reproducing a decoder from discrete motif IDs and boundary angles.

The generative evidence is preliminary: the main comparison uses only 100 samples per model, with 1 versus 3–4 designable samples and no uncertainty estimates. The scaling experiment also changes the length protocol from an average of approximately 214 residues to 50–128 residues, confounding the attribution of improved designability to additional data and parameters.

Important experimental details remain unclear despite extensive pseudocode, particularly downstream training settings and exact storage accounting. Algorithm 6 also samples at most 5000 occurrences by default but requires K distinct initial medoids, while reported configurations request up to 20000; the handling of this incompatibility is unspecified. Overall, the promising idea is not yet supported by sufficiently reliable and controlled evidence for acceptance.

strengths: The combination of geometric medoid prototypes, hierarchical merging, and inverse-kinematics refinement is an interesting, interpretable approach to protein structure tokenization.

The evaluation is broad, covering reconstruction, downstream prediction, data efficiency, generation, and tokenization of 550K structures. The small-data reconstruction results and several downstream improvements are promising.

The glue-refinement ablation provides concrete support for this component: removing it increases RMSD from 1.66 to 4.39. Extensive pseudocode, hyperparameter documentation, and runtime measurements are also useful.
weaknesses: The downstream comparisons do not isolate the proposed hierarchy's contribution. GEOBPE-TRANSFER adds a trainable bidirectional TreeLSTM to ESM3 features, whereas the baseline uses ESM3 representations directly. Matched-capacity controls using random or balanced trees, secondary-structure partitions, and ordinary sequence aggregation are needed. Performance is also not consistently superior: average flexibility correlation trails both continuous baselines, and repeat prediction deteriorates substantially.

The near-perfect domain agreement does not establish that individual tokens recover functional domains. Appendix G selects the best union of arbitrarily many consecutive segments for each annotated domain; sufficiently fine partitions can achieve nearly perfect scores without discovering domain structure. Moreover, Table 2 describes parenthetical values as random-baseline percentiles, while Appendix G describes them as average baseline scores. Direct boundary metrics and clearly specified length-matched controls are necessary.

Compression claims need more transparent accounting. BPR includes the entire tokenizer's description length, making comparisons sensitive to model serialization and the corpus over which that cost is amortized. The paper does not provide an auditable breakdown of model/codebook storage versus motif and glue-token payload. Figure 4 also shows materially lower reconstruction fidelity than ProToken and ESM3, so the abstract's claim of over 10× compression at similar distortion is not established by a matched-distortion comparison.

The central hierarchical-merging contribution is insufficiently connected to the strongest reconstruction results. Table 16's vocabulary sizes of 600, 2500, 6000, and 21000 equal the corresponding initialization codebook sizes, and Appendix K reports negligible merging at high resolution. A direct comparison against initialization plus glue optimization, with token-length and merge statistics, is needed to establish benefits beyond residue-level geometric quantization.

Generation claims overstate the evidence. Section 5 describes 99% unique and designable backbones, but Table 11 reports 98–99% uniqueness and only 3–4% designability for the small models. With 100 samples and no uncertainty estimates, this is weak evidence of a reliable designability improvement over 1%. The scaling experiment additionally changes evaluation lengths from roughly 214 residues to 50–128, confounding attribution of the reported improvement to scale.

The geometric specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3.1 defines G_i = F_{i+1}F_i^{-1}, while subsequent forward kinematics uses F_{i+1} = F_iG_i; these are incompatible conventions, and the former transform is not determined solely by invariant internal coordinates as claimed. Algorithm 12 also changes the glue variables and appears to optimize every residue link, leaving unclear how merged motif interiors remain fixed and exactly decodable from their prototypes.

Despite substantial appendix detail, downstream training specifications and repeated-run uncertainty are insufficient. Together with the unresolved comparison and metric issues, this prevents the promising idea from meeting the evidence standard for acceptance.
